title: Achilles and Priam
text:
Achilles had killed Hector, the greatest warrior of Troy, to avenge his friend Patroclus. For days he dragged Hector's body behind his chariot around Patroclus's tomb. The gods protected the body from decay, and at last Zeus sent word that Achilles must give it back.

Old King Priam, Hector's father, set out at night with a wagon of treasure for the ransom. Guided by the god Hermes, he passed unseen through the Greek camp and walked into Achilles's hut. He fell at Achilles's knees and kissed his hands, the terrible hands that had killed so many of his sons.

"Remember your own father," Priam said, "an old man like me." He told Achilles that he had done what no man on earth had done before: kissed the hands of the man who killed his son.

The words moved Achilles. He took the old man's hand, and the two of them wept together, Priam for Hector, Achilles for his father and for Patroclus. Then Achilles lifted Priam up, had Hector's body washed and wrapped, and himself laid it on the wagon. They ate together and looked at each other in wonder. Achilles promised a truce of eleven days for Hector's funeral, and the Iliad ends with the burial of Hector, tamer of horses.
lesson: Shared grief can break through even deep hostility. When you are in conflict, remember that the other side has fathers, sons and losses too.
